title: Mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind: readiness, costs and risks
label: 29 October 2026 · Mandatory payrolling of benefits in kind
summary: Witnesses from payroll professionals, payroll-software providers and the CBI gave a mixed verdict on the Government’s plan to force employers to report most employee benefits through payroll in real time. They warned the phased roll-out will increase workload and errors in the short term, that many employers and software suppliers are not ready, and that HMRC’s IT and engagement have been inadequate. They urged more testing, clearer guidance, an extended penalty soft-landing and a rethink about simplification and investment in HMRC systems.

chapters.title: What the change is and who was speaking
chapters.takeaway: The witnesses explained the Government wants most benefits reported through payroll in real time, and set out who they represent.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Today we are looking at the Government’s proposal to make reporting most benefits in kind mandatory in payroll, replacing much of the P11D process.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: I represent BASDA, the trade body for business software developers; our PAYE special interest group is focused on these changes.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: I’m from the Chartered Institute of Payroll Professionals (CIPP); I’ve also worked inside HMRC on this project.

turns.speaker: Andy Scott
turns.text: I’m the CBI’s principal tax adviser; our members range from small firms to large groups, and I run the employment taxes working group.

chapters.title: Short-term impact and readiness
chapters.takeaway: All three witnesses said the short-term effect will likely be more burden, errors and confusion because many employers and software providers aren’t ready.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: This is a phased move but it changes where work happens: instead of an annual P11D, employers must handle the same work across each pay period, and that creates friction.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: Payroll software is designed for pay, not benefits valuation and HR data. Most employers expect software to solve everything, but many are unprepared and the data often sits with benefit providers or HR.

turns.speaker: Andy Scott
turns.text: It’s a mixed picture: some businesses have voluntarily payrolled benefits for years and will be fine, others—especially with complex benefit structures—face a big task and need more time.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: Payroll outsourcers and accountancy firms will also be affected: revenue from P11D work may move into payroll services, increasing ongoing costs for employers.

chapters.title: Consultation, testing and the timeline
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses said HMRC engagement, detailed technical specifications and testing have been too slow; they urged more time and better testing before April.

turns.speaker: Baroness Wheatcroft
turns.text: This has been planned for some time. Given the lack of effective consultation, can the April deadline be met and what should the Government do now?

turns.speaker: Andy Scott
turns.text: HMRC’s policy team has engaged, but the detailed technical specs for software arrived late. Many members say five or six months’ notice for specs is insufficient; some need 12 months.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: We asked to meet HMRC regularly from early 2024 but weren’t taken up. Crucial things like end-to-end testing were delayed; the main HMRC test system only became available after supplier changes.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: Software suppliers need time to implement and to get into employer systems. Many employers have a year-end or Christmas code freeze when they won’t accept changes.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: The crunch is now: software must know exactly what to implement for employers to be educated. Communications so far risk telling employers there’s a small RTI change when it’s much bigger.

turns.speaker: Baroness Bi
turns.text: Given code freezes and late specs, would you recommend pushing the deadline from April 2027 to April 2028?

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: Politically a further delay is unlikely because of Treasury costings, but practical reliefs and administrative easements should be considered.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: Phase 2 should be deferred: learn from phase 1 and fix the end-of-year process before piling on more complex items like loans and accommodation.

chapters.title: Costs, parallel systems and penalties
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses challenged HMRC’s low cost estimates, warned employers may run systems in parallel for years, and urged an extended penalty soft-landing.

turns.speaker: Lord Carrington of Fulham
turns.text: With some benefits excluded until later, firms may need to run P11D and payroll reporting in parallel. That seems costly and complex—what about HMRC’s £8 million estimate?

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: That £8 million looks wildly low. From software industry experience we estimate the real cost could be several times higher—perhaps fivefold—because this is a new business function, not a small RTI tweak.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: Employers face additional software, admin and reconciliation costs. The supposed one-off saving is mainly the removed P11D fee, but the ongoing burden may just spread across the year.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: HMRC’s numbers implied just a few dozen pounds per employer. That’s implausible given the hours and specialist staff some firms have already spent.

turns.speaker: Andy Scott
turns.text: One member has quantified 3,500 hours of implementation work, costing far more than HMRC’s implied per-employer figure. There is a big gulf between HMRC’s model and businesses’ experience.

turns.speaker: Lord Newby
turns.text: HMRC plans a penalty soft-landing in year one. Will that be enough?

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: Soft-landing needs extending through the phased roll-out and year-end process. Penalties should be reserved for deliberate non-compliance, not honest mistakes in a rushed transition.

chapters.title: Recommendations and closing points
chapters.takeaway: Witnesses urged better HMRC engagement, more testing, administrative easements, simplification of benefit rules, and investment in modern HMRC systems.

turns.speaker: Andy Scott
turns.text: Policymakers should step back and look across the system: simplify rules where possible, consider more flexible PAYE settlement agreements and update legacy allowances to reduce reporting volumes.

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: We urged HMRC to engage closely with software providers and benefit suppliers and to invest in better data-exchange systems; RTI is showing its age.

turns.speaker: Mathew Akrigg
turns.text: Practical steps: clearer employer guidance, targeted easements for firms and software providers that cannot be ready, and an extended penalty soft-landing.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you. Is there anything you want to add that you haven’t said?

turns.speaker: Kevin Hart
turns.text: Only that HMRC needs to be honest about the scale of change and fund the right systems and engagement: otherwise this will be a costly, stressful transition for employers and the tax authority alike.

turns.speaker: Chair
turns.text: Thank you to all three witnesses for a thorough session. The committee will reflect on these points as we prepare our report.
